paper.title: Modeling and numerical simulations of dendritic crystal growth

blocks.source_text: The work seeks a minimal model that can generate diverse dendritic morphologies. It deliberately excludes convection and expansion or shrinkage caused by phase transition and focuses on crystal morphology.

Explicit interface tracking becomes complicated when interfaces merge or separate and is difficult to extend to three dimensions. The proposed phase field instead represents a finite-thickness interface implicitly over the whole domain.

The model uses phase field p(r,t), with p=0 liquid and p=1 solid, and temperature T(r,t). A steep transition in p represents the solid-liquid interface; epsilon controls layer thickness and interface mobility, and F is a double-well potential.
Ginzburg-Landau free energy and the quartic double-well potential F(p;m), visually verified on PDF page 2.
Anisotropic phase-field evolution equation (3), with orientation-dependent epsilon and the double-well reaction term, visually verified on PDF page 3.
The singular limit relates normal velocity to thermodynamic driving, curvature, and orientation-dependent surface tension; epsilon-bar is a computational interface-thickness parameter.
The thermodynamic driving m is a bounded function of supercooling, while sigma(theta)=1+delta cos[j(theta-theta0)] defines anisotropy strength, mode, and orientation.
Enthalpy conservation gives a heat equation in which K times the phase-field rate is a latent-heat source localized at the moving interface; visually verified on PDF page 4.

Two-dimensional calculations use square 9x9 or rectangular 12x3 domains, 300x300 or 400x100 meshes, epsilon-bar=0.01, tau=0.0003, alpha=0.9, gamma=10, noise amplitude 0.01, and time step 0.0002. Equation (3) is explicit and equation (5) implicit; p has zero-flux boundaries.
Figure 7 shows that increasing four-fold anisotropy delta from 0 to 0.050 changes growth from isotropic fingering through mixed forms to strongly oriented dendrites with screening and side branching.
Figures 10 and 11 connect side-branch sensitivity to noise and show how the anisotropic capillary function d0(theta) can become negative, corresponding to corner formation.

Noise changes competition and selection among side branches without changing main-tip velocity in the non-oscillating case; oscillatory tip growth provides a stronger side-branch mechanism and reduces noise sensitivity.

Even small anisotropy can strongly influence growth because derivatives in the capillary function amplify angular modes. The coupled equations reproduce many realistic crystal morphologies over the sampled parameter subset.

Structures at or below the diffuse-interface thickness cannot be resolved; narrow slits are buried. Quantitative interface velocity requires epsilon/dx and tau/dt sufficiently large, but the reported meshes were selected for qualitative morphology rather than precise velocity.
The snowflake-like simulations represent supercooled water solidification, not vapor-grown snowflakes; vapor growth would require facet formation and destabilization mechanisms absent from the model.
The official ScienceDirect record confirms the title, author, journal, volume, issue, pages, date, and DOI but does not identify an author code, data, or executable-model deposit.
